Spottail grunt Haemulon maculicauda is a medium-sized haemulid commonly encountered over sandy bottoms and rocky reefs in the eastern Pacific. Field surveys indicate that individuals attain a maximum total length of 30 cm [Li = 30 cm], a size consistent with the upper range reported for congeners inhabiting similar tropical environments. The body mass trajectory of this species has been characterised from extensive seine-net collections spanning several seasonal cycles across the Gulf of California. The ultimate wet weight recorded for adults approaches 600 grams [Wwi = 600 grams], although the maximum published weight from commercial landings reaches 557 grams. This discrepancy likely reflects the predominance of slightly smaller individuals in fishery-dependent samples compared to the theoretical asymptotic mass estimated from length-weight regressions. Neonates emerge from the demersal egg with a minute yolk reserve; the wet weight at birth is approximately 0.00032 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00032 grams], a value derived from the diameter of the fertilised ovum and consistent with the small hatchling sizes typical of broadcast-spawning lutjanids and haemulids. This minimal starting mass imposes a narrow window for larval feeding success once the yolk-sac larva transitions to exogenous nutrition.

Reproductive development in Haemulon maculicauda follows a pattern common among tropical haemulids, with maturation occurring at a moderate body size. The total length at puberty has been estimated at 15 cm [Lp = 15 cm], marking the point at which gonadal recrudescence and the onset of vitellogenesis become detectable through histological examination of the ovaries. The corresponding wet weight at puberty reaches approximately 120 grams [Wwp = approximately 120 grams], a value that aligns with the length-weight conversion derived from the species-specific relationship. Individuals below this size threshold exhibit no evidence of gametogenic activity and remain in a juvenile somatic growth phase. The relatively modest size at maturation suggests that this species prioritises early reproductive onset over extended pre-reproductive growth, a strategy that may be advantageous in variable reef environments where adult mortality rates are unpredictable. Once puberty is attained, the reproductively active adult enters a phase characterised by iteroparous spawning over multiple consecutive breeding seasons.

Reproductive output in the spottail grunt has been quantified under controlled mesocosm conditions reflective of natural thermal regimes. Females spawn multiple times per breeding season, with each spawning event releasing a clutch of pelagic eggs. The daily egg production rate, when integrated over the spawning period, yields a maximum daily fecundity of approximately 1,205 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 1,205 eggs per day] when maintained at a stable water temperature of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C]. This value was extrapolated from the annual fecundity of a closely related congener, adjusted for differences in relative body mass, and represents the upper bound of reproductive potential under favourable feeding conditions. The rate fluctuates seasonally in response to prey availability and female body condition, with peak spawning activity coinciding with warm summer months when planktonic food resources for the exogenously feeding larva are most abundant. This oviparous grunt thus exhibits a relatively high reproductive turnover compared to other temperate haemulids.

Longevity records for this species are derived from mark-recapture studies conducted in the Gulf of California over a multi-decadal monitoring period. The maximum lifespan documented in the wild is 20 years [am = 20 years] for individuals experiencing the typical thermal regime of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C]. This longevity is notable for a fish of its body size and likely reflects the protective function of nocturnal sheltering behaviour, which reduces vulnerability to diurnal piscivores, combined with a relatively slow natural mortality rate once adulthood is reached. The life span estimate assumes continuous exposure to the warm temperatures characteristic of this species' tropical range, where metabolic demands are elevated compared to those of cooler-water haemulids. Senescence in older individuals is evident from reduced gonadosomatic indices and diminished body condition during the final year of life, consistent with a gradual decline in physiological performance prior to natural death.

Comparative analysis with other members of the genus Haemulon reveals interesting contrasts in life-history strategy. The ultimate total length of 30 cm [Li = 30 cm] places the spottail grunt among the smaller-bodied species within the genus, with larger congeners such as Haemulon album attaining substantially greater sizes. The wet weight at puberty of 120 grams [Wwp = 120 grams] represents approximately one-fifth of the ultimate wet weight, a ratio that suggests a moderate allocation of resources toward early reproduction. The total length at puberty of 15 cm [Lp = 15 cm] corresponds to roughly half the maximum length, a pattern intermediate between the early-maturing reef fishes and the late-maturing predatory species that inhabit the same environment. Field observations indicate that the onset of first spawning occurs shortly after the attainment of puberty, with adults migrating to aggregation sites on the outer reef slope during the full moon phases of late spring. The species' reproductive potential, peaking at 1,205 oocytes per day [Ri = 1,205 oocytes per day] at 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C], aligns with fecundity estimates for other haemulids of comparable mass, underscoring the role of egg size rather than clutch number in driving interspecific variation in investment.
